'''''Fuchsia magellanica''''' – commonly known as the '''hummingbird fuchsia''', '''hardy fuchsia''' or '''chilco''' (from {{langx|arn|chillko}} "watery"<ref>{{cite dictionary|year=1846|entry=chillco|dictionary=Diccionario Chileno Hispano|url=https://www.scielo.cl/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0718-93032010000200008|first=Andrés|last=Febrés|place=Santiago|publisher=Imprenta de los Tribunales|page=448|access-date=10 February 2025|archive-date=29 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240329141508/https://www.scielo.cl/scielo.php?pid=S0718-93032010000200008&script=sci_arttext|url-status=live}}</ref>) – is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the evening primrose [[family (botany)|family]] [[Onagraceae]], native to the lower [[Southern Cone]] of southern [[South America]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=FUMA |title=USDA |publisher=Plants.usda.gov |date=1989-03-02 |access-date=2018-10-09 |archive-date=4 November 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111104230720/http://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=FUMA |url-status=live }}</ref> 

==Description==
[[File:Fuchsia Magellanica Tas.jpg|thumb|180px|left|''Fuchsia magellanica'' - flower]]
This [[sub-shrub]]  with long, arcuate stems can grow to {{convert|1-3|m|ft}} in height and width in frost-free climates, and {{Convert abbreviated|1.2-1.5|m|ft|0}} where colder. Its leaves grow in whorls of 3–4 per node or sometimes opposite, are ovate to lanceolate, 2.5–6 cm long, and 1–2 cm wide, with serrate margins and petioles 0.5–1 cm long. The plant blossoms profusely over a long period with many small and tubular pendent flowers, in brilliant shades of red and purple, softer shades of pink and lavender, and some in white. The perfect flowers are axillary and pendent, with peduncles 3–4.5 cm long, a magenta floral tube 10–13 mm long, magenta sepals 20–25 mm long, and dark purple petals 10–13 mm long that become convolute after anthesis. The stamens are exserted, with filaments 25–30 mm long. The berries are ellipsoid, 10–15 mm long and 0.7–0.9 mm wide.<ref name="Species Page/ Botany, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution n714">{{cite web | title=Onagraceae | website=Species Page/ Botany, National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution | url=https://naturalhistory2.si.edu/botany/onagraceae/speciesdescr.cfm?myID=3645 | access-date=2024-04-22 | archive-date=2 December 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241202232019/https://naturalhistory2.si.edu/botany/onagraceae/speciesdescr.cfm?myID=3645 | url-status=live }}</ref> Chromosome count is 2n = 44.<ref name="Berry 1989 p. 532">{{cite journal | last=Berry | first=Paul E. | title=A Systematic Revision of Fuchsia Sect. Quelusia (Onagraceae) | journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden | volume=76 | issue=2 | date=1989 | doi=10.2307/2399499 | page=532}}</ref>

''F. magellanica'' is a consistently variable species across the whole of its natural range and, despite past usage and popular misconceptions, no scientific varieties are currently recognized by botanist Dr. Paul E. Berry, the leading authority on the genus.<ref>Paul E. Berry. “A Systematic Revision of Fuchsia Sect. Quelusia (Onagraceae).” ''Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden'', 1989, Vol. 76, No. 2, pp. 532-584.</ref> Care should be taken not to accord any of the many garden selections and hybrids with taxonomic status by using "var." Additionally, pollen stain tests conducted in the [[Pacific Northwest]] region of the United States by members of the Western Fuchsia Species Society have indicated that almost all of the many garden selections of this species are, in fact, hybrids to a lesser or greater degree.

It is distinguished from other species in the section by its elongated ovary and fruit, long petioles that are usually over 1/4 the length of the blade, and highly dentate leaf margins.<ref name="Berry 1989 p. 532"/>

==Distribution==
This species of ''[[Fuchsia]]'' occurs in [[temperate climate|temperate]] southern regions of [[Argentina]] and [[Chile]], from [[latitude]] 32°50' S.  to the [[Straits of Magellan]]. ''Fuchsia magellenica'' thrives in damp scrublands, forest edges, or clearings, often close to water sources. It is geographically isolated from the Brazilian species of the ''Quelusia'' section by a distance of 1000-1500 km. In Australia, the species is recorded as naturalized in the states of [[Western Australia]], [[South Australia]], [[New South Wales]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] and [[Tasmania]].<ref name=APNI>{{APNI|name=''Fuchsia magellanica'' Lam.|id=11209}}</ref><ref name="Berry 1989 p. 532"/>

Naturalised in south west Ireland, a common sight in hedgerows, so much so that the flower has become the emblem of West Cork.

== Cultivation and uses ==
[[File:Fuchsia_de_Magellan_.JPG|thumb|200px|left|Planted in a hedge]]
They arrived in England in the late 18th century. According to tradition, the English gardener James Lee discovered them on the windowsill of a seaman's house and bought them for a considerable sum. As early as 1793 Lee is said to have sold a large number of pieces that he had pulled from this one copy. ''Fuchsia magellanica'', and its [[cultivar]]s and [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]]s, are widely cultivated by plant nurseries and gardeners as [[ornamental plant]]s. They are grown in temperate and [[subtropical]] gardens and conservatories, in containers on patios, balconies, and indoors. They prefer a sunny position.

The plants are quite cold-hardy compared to other species from more [[tropical climate]]s, being deciduous where frosts are light, and only top die back in hard frosts (with [[mulch]]ing).  The profuse drooping flowers are a [[nectar]] source attractive to [[hummingbird]]s.<ref>"Sunset Western Garden Book" - ''Fuchsia magellanica'' entry; Lane Publishing; 7th edition 2001.</ref>

This species, and hybrids using it as parent stock, are very susceptible to the fuchsia [[gall mite]], ''Aculops fuchsiae'', a serious disfiguring pest that was first accidentally spread from its native Brazil to the West Coast of the United States in 1980. It has more recently made appearances in France (2003), the Channel Islands (2006) and the United Kingdom (2007). Fortunately the fuchsia gall mite does not readily survive temperatures below {{convert|4|C|F|abbr=on}}, and there are effective treatments and strategies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.americanfuchsiasociety.org/fuchsiaarticles/fuchsiagallmite4-2004.html|access-date=2 May 2023|website=American Fuchsia Society|date=May 2004|author=Rodney Bergquist|title=Food for Thought Regarding Fuchsia Gall Mites|archive-date=14 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714143731/http://www.americanfuchsiasociety.org/fuchsiaarticles/fuchsiagallmite4-2004.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It has been used in traditional remedies as a diuretic and antipyretic.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chilco / Fucsia|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100401034044/http://www.redsalud.gov.cl/portal/url/item/7d983cf52cf08bd6e04001011e011da0.pdf|url=http://www.redsalud.gov.cl/portal/url/item/7d983cf52cf08bd6e04001011e011da0.pdf|archive-date=Apr 1, 2010|website=Medicamentos herbarios Tradicionales|language=es|publisher=Chilean Ministry of Health}}</ref>
